subject: Civil Engineering
title: Ronan Point: The Progressive Collapse
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Ronan Point: The Progressive Collapse.

hook.text: In 1968, a gas explosion in one flat brought down an entire corner of a tower block.

buildup.text: Ronan Point was a precast panel building — walls stacked like a house of cards.

discovery.text: Removing one panel eliminated support for everything above it. Floors fell in series.

twist.text: The building met every code at the time. Codes never considered progressive collapse.

climax.text: After Ronan Point, building codes worldwide added rules for alternate load paths.

punchline.text: One panel failed and the building unzipped itself floor by floor.

quiz.question: What is progressive collapse?
options: Gradual settling of a building's foundation over decades
One local failure triggers a chain reaction that collapses a larger portion
A building slowly leaning to one side due to uneven loads

details.summary: On May 16, 1968, a gas explosion in an 18th-floor flat of the Ronan Point tower block in London blew out a load-bearing wall panel. Without that panel, the floors above collapsed one by one, and each falling floor knocked out the panels below.
details.whyItMatters: Ronan Point introduced the concept of progressive collapse to structural engineering and led to requirements that all buildings must have alternate load paths to prevent disproportionate collapse from localized damage.
takeaways: A single panel failure triggered cascading collapse of the entire building corner
Large-panel precast systems lacked connections to tie the structure together
Building codes now require structural robustness and alternate load paths

faq.question: What is progressive collapse and how is it prevented?
faq.answer: Progressive collapse occurs when local failure triggers a chain reaction of failures that causes damage disproportionate to the initial cause. It is prevented by designing connections that tie the structure together so if one member fails, loads redistribute through alternate paths.

faq.question: What changes did the Ronan Point collapse bring to building codes?
faq.answer: The UK immediately required structural ties in all buildings over five stories. International codes adopted requirements for structural integrity, tie forces, and alternate load path analysis.
